title: Headwaters: Snow to Flow
text:
Most of the water in the upper Rio Grande starts as mountain snow. This page compares the peak snowpack at high-elevation SNOTEL sites, and when it melts, with the water that passed the first river gage below each headwater basin, for water years 1987 through 2026 (each runs October through September). Data run through September 30, 2026.
A snow site measures one point high on a mountain. A stream gage measures everything that flows past it from the whole basin above. Snow sites sit where snow is deep and lasts, and much of each basin sits lower and holds less snow per acre, so their readings work as an index of how snowy a year was, not a measure of how much water the whole snowpack holds. Pairing two snow sites per basin is a judgment about which points best stand for that basin. For the Rio Chama, I average Cumbres Trestle (the upper Chama) with Hopewell in the Tusas Mountains, which stands in for the Rio Brazos side. The two halves each supply roughly half of the river’s summer flow at La Puente. Years of hiking and running trails between Beartown and Hopewell have given me a feel for these even splits, which step from south to north in neighboring pairs: Hopewell and Cumbres Trestle for the Chama, Cumbres Trestle and Wolf Creek Summit for the Conejos, and Wolf Creek Summit and Beartown for the upper Rio Grande.

title: Headwaters: Snow to Flow
section: The Chama lost the most snow, and the most water
text:
The Chama lost the most snow, and the most water



Comparing the first 20 years of the shared record (1987–2006) with the last 20 (2007–2026), median peak snowpack fell 18% on the Rio Chama, 13% on the Conejos and 15% on the upper Rio Grande. Median water-year flow fell 27%, 6% and 1%.
The Chama’s flow has always swung harder than its snow: in 1987–2006, each 1% change in its snowpack came with about a 1.5% change in flow, because soils, plants and evaporation take their share of the melt first. The Conejos and the upper Rio Grande tracked their snow about one for one. Measured against how each river responded to its snowpack in 1987–2006, all three delivered about what their snow predicted in 2007–2026. The Rio Chama came in 5% under that expectation, the Conejos even with it and the upper Rio Grande 6% over, all within normal year-to-year variation.

title: Headwaters: Snow to Flow
text:
Flow still follows snow



Each dot is one water year. In all three basins, recent years mostly fall among earlier years with similar snowpacks. More of them sit at the low-snow end.

title: Headwaters: Snow to Flow
text:
The snow melts earlier



At all four snow sites, the snowpack now peaks lower and is half gone 6 to 14 days earlier in spring than in 1987–2006. Much of that is simply less snow: each inch less at the peak brings the half-gone date about one to one and a half days earlier. Comparing years with similar snowpacks, only Wolf Creek Summit melts clearly earlier, by about 9 days. It’s also the site that used to melt latest, half gone in early June.
In 2026 the snowpack peaked in early March at all four sites, among the earliest peaks since 1987. At Beartown, Cumbres Trestle and Hopewell it was half gone by late March, two to nearly three weeks earlier than in any other year since 1987.

title: Headwaters: Snow to Flow
text:
Seventy years at La Puente



The La Puente gage has measured the Rio Chama since 1955. It sits upstream of El Vado Reservoir and of the point where San Juan–Chama Project water enters the river, so its flows contain no imported water. Water year 2026 (provisional) brought 80 thousand acre-feet, about 35% of the 1991–2020 median of 228.

title: Headwaters: Snow to Flow
section: What this shows, and what it doesn’t
text:
What this shows, and what it doesn’t
All three headwater rivers carried less water after 2006, about as much less as their smaller snowpacks predict, and the Rio Chama lost the most of both. None of the three is delivering clearly less than its snowpack predicts. Snow at all four sites also melts earlier. At three of them that matches their smaller snowpacks; only Wolf Creek Summit melts clearly earlier for the same amount of snow.
Things to keep in mind:

The Chama’s snow index matters. With Cumbres Trestle alone, the Chama looks like it now makes less water per inch of snow: 13% less than Cumbres predicts, with a statistically significant downward trend. With both halves of the basin represented, it doesn’t. Any blend that gives the Hopewell side at least 30% of the weight shows no significant shortfall.
On the Conejos and the upper Rio Grande, flow fell less than snow (6% vs. 13%, and 1% vs. 15%), even though both rivers have historically tracked their snow about one for one. That’s within normal variation. It could mean these basins kept more of their snow than the high sites near the Continental Divide show, or that rain, groundwater and reservoir releases made up part of the difference. These data can’t tell which.
The Chama’s snow sites sit lower, and so does its basin. Cumbres Trestle and Hopewell sit near 10,000 feet, Wolf Creek Summit near 10,900 and Beartown near 11,600. Less than 4% of the Chama basin above La Puente lies above 11,000 feet, compared with 35–41% of the Conejos and upper Rio Grande basins, and the Chama has no higher SNOTEL site. Within their own basins the two pairs sit at similar heights: about two-thirds of the Chama basin lies below Cumbres Trestle and Hopewell, and 56–78% of the upper Rio Grande basin lies below Wolf Creek Summit and Beartown.
The flow numbers don’t depend on any of these choices. Wherever the record is split, from 1997 to 2016, the Chama’s median flow fell 27–46%, while the other two rivers’ fell at most 23%.







NoteMethods and data





Snow. NRCS SNOTEL daily snow water equivalent at Cumbres Trestle (431:CO:SNTL), Hopewell (532:NM:SNTL), Wolf Creek Summit (874:CO:SNTL) and Beartown (327:CO:SNTL). Each basin’s index averages two sites’ daily values (both must report), then takes the year’s peak. A year needs at least 250 days of snow data before July 1.
The Chama’s snow index. Hopewell sits about 2 km outside the basin, just over the ridge from the Rio Brazos drainage, and stands in for the Rio Brazos side; Cumbres Trestle sits on the divide at the head of the upper Chama. Seasonal gages on the upper Chama (above Chama) and the Rio Brazos (at Fishtail Road), running since 2014, show each supplying roughly a third to a half of La Puente’s May–September flow. In years when Hopewell is snowier relative to Cumbres, the Brazos carries a larger share (rank correlation 0.77 over 10 summers). Over 1987–2026, the Cumbres–Hopewell average explains 80% of the year-to-year variation in La Puente’s flow; Cumbres alone explains 73%. Giving Cumbres anywhere from 0% to 70% of the weight shows no significant shortfall; 80% or more does.
Flow. USGS daily mean discharge at Rio Chama near La Puente (08284100), Conejos River near Mogote (08246500) and Rio Grande near Del Norte (08220000). USGS daily values for the two Colorado gages end in December 2024; from January 2025 this page uses the Colorado Division of Water Resources’ reviewed record (CONMOGCO, RIODELCO). Water-year flow is the sum of daily mean flow times 1.983471 acre-feet per cfs-day, for years with at least 360 days of record. Flows are as measured at the gage, not adjusted for upstream reservoirs or diversions.
Expected flow. Each river’s water-year flow is fit against its snow index for 1987–2006 (a straight-line fit) and applied to each 2007–2026 snowpack. “Within normal year-to-year variation” means inside the range where the 20-year average would fall 90% of the time if the 1987–2006 relationship still held.
Melt timing. NRCS SNOTEL daily snow water equivalent at each site, smoothed with a 3-day median to remove one-day sensor spikes, for water years with at least 90% of days from October 1 to August 31. Half gone: the first day after each year’s peak when snow water equivalent falls to half of that peak. Chart dates are medians of the yearly dates. Trends 1987–2026 (Sen slope, Kendall test): half gone earlier by 6.5 days per decade at Wolf Creek Summit, 4.6 at Beartown and 3.3 at Hopewell; Cumbres Trestle’s 2.6 isn’t significant. Holding peak snowpack fixed, Wolf Creek Summit is about 9 days earlier in 2007–2026 (90% range 4–14 days); the other three sites are about 2–3 days earlier, within year-to-year variation. Half-gone dates vary by about two weeks from year to year (standard deviation 12–17 days).
Elevations. Site elevations from NRCS station metadata. Basin elevations from USGS NLDI basin outlines and AWS Terrain Tiles (about 120 m); the outlined areas match USGS drainage areas within 2%. The 10,000-foot pair (Cumbres Trestle, Hopewell) and the 11,000-foot pair (Wolf Creek Summit, Beartown) rise and fall together (rank correlation 0.83), and the lower pair hasn’t lost ground against the higher one (no significant trend, 1987–2026). By site, peak snowpack fell most at Hopewell (22% by median, 18% by average); the other three don’t line up by elevation. The two lower sites are also the two southernmost, so elevation and latitude can’t be separated.
Periods. Water years 1987–2006 and 2007–2026: equal 20-year halves of the record all three basins share. Wolf Creek Summit’s first full season is 1987.
La Puente chart. LOESS: locally linear, frac = 0.2, robust. Moving average: 10-year exponentially weighted, trailing only. Median: 1991–2020.
Limits. Water years 2025 and 2026 are provisional. Flows at Mogote and Del Norte are affected by upstream reservoirs (Platoro; Rio Grande Reservoir) and small transbasin imports. Two snow sites stand in for each basin, and only Beartown sits clearly inside the basin it stands for. Cumbres Trestle sits on the upper Chama’s divide, and Wolf Creek Summit on the Continental Divide (on the San Juan side, by NRCS’s watershed code). Hopewell sits about 2 km outside the Chama basin, and neither Conejos site is inside the Conejos basin above Mogote (Cumbres Trestle is about 6 km outside, Wolf Creek Summit about 18 km).
